principles.quote: we can mix and match to adjust our long or short exposure for a 1-point stock movement.

rule.action: compute net position delta and adjust

principles.chapter: The Subprime Mortgage Crisis and Options
principles.subsection: Delta Relationships of Stocks and Options
principles.principle: Delta/gamma hedges can be thrown completely out of sync by gaps at the open or after halts.
principles.quote: Traders know that their positions may become completely out of sync on these occasions, rendering their strategies worthless and subjecting them to increased risk.

rule.action: recompute hedges after gaps; warn on gap risk

principles.chapter: The Subprime Mortgage Crisis and Options
principles.subsection: Delta Relationships of Stocks and Options
principles.principle: Use deltas to hedge odd-lot positions (e.g., 674 shares vs eight 0.84-delta ITM calls = 672 deltas).
principles.quote: The trader may create a delta neutral strategy by selling eight in-the-money calls with a delta of 0.84, yielding an offsetting position of 672 deltas to the 674 long deltas

rule.action: size option hedge by delta

principles.chapter: The Subprime Mortgage Crisis and Options
principles.subsection: Delta Relationships of Stocks and Options
principles.principle: The safer the position, the less it can make; balance risk across positions and adjust hedges as conditions change.
principles.quote: The safer the positions, the less money an investor can make.

rule.action: present risk/return tradeoff

principles.chapter: The Subprime Mortgage Crisis and Options
principles.subsection: Delta Relationships of Stocks and Options
principles.principle: Fund managers can use Bollinger Bands (two SD around the 20-day MA) on daily charts to watch extremes and volatility instead of tick charts.
principles.quote: Bollinger Bands are normally placed two standard deviations both above and below a stock’s 20-day moving average

rule.action: daily monitoring of extremes

principles.principle: Theta (daily decay) increases toward expiration; check decay across three-day holiday weekends when timing buys and sells.
principles.quote: I often monitor theta over three-day holiday weekends.

rule.action: estimate weekend decay = theta x calendar days (e.g., 3)

principles.principle: Use theta to decide how long before an event to buy options.
principles.quote: Or you might wonder whether you should purchase an option two weeks before an event, or how long you should wait before making that purchase

rule.action: compare decay cost vs expected pre-event move

principles.principle: Vega: as volatility increases, both put and call premiums rise; vega applies to individual contracts.
principles.quote: As volatility increases, so do premiums for both puts and calls, though at different levels for each option contract.

rule.action: report position vega

principles.principle: Rho: rising rates lift calls and lower puts; falling rates do the reverse.
principles.quote: Rising rates normally lift call premiums and reduce put premiums.

rule.action: report rho; many vendors omit it

principles.principle: FLEX options allow custom strike, expiry (to five years, not within three days of standard expiration) and American/European style; American usually costs slightly more.
principles.quote: American-style options usually have slightly higher premiums than their European-style equivalents.

rule.action: note exercise-style premium difference

principles.principle: Dividend capture: before the ex-date buy spot-month ITM calls with little or no time premium (or below parity), exercise, collect the dividend, then sell the shares.
principles.quote: Traders often buy these contracts within the spot expiration month, with little or no time premium, or at a discount to their intrinsic value.

rule.condition: before ex-date; ITM call time value ~0 or negative
rule.action: buy ITM call, exercise before ex-date
rule.notes: Option volume jumps around ex-dividend dates.

principles.principle: In ex-dividend call spreads, if the short call is exercised before the trader exercises the long, there is no dividend capture.
principles.quote: If the short option is exercised ahead of the dividend and before the trader exercises the long call, the stock would change hands before becoming ex-dividend, yielding a flat position with no dividend capture.

rule.action: warn: assignment risk defeats dividend capture

principles.principle: Buy straddles/strangles (e.g., before earnings) only when implied volatility is low; high premiums require larger moves to break even.
principles.quote: Straddles and strangles strategies let traders participate in strong movements regardless of direction, but they are normally used only when implied volatility levels are low.

rule.action: allow long straddle/strangle only in low-IV regime

principles.subsection: Getting Information from the Exchange Floor
principles.principle: When options look out of line, find out why (dividend changes, currency effects, takeover or FDA rumors) before trading.
principles.quote: It seemed that some of the options were out of line with the market— especially in the put contracts, which were trading well above anticipated levels.

rule.action: warn: investigate before trading

principles.principle: Example covered-call fund guidelines: premium at least 4% of the stock price and at least 2.5% upside to the strike.
principles.quote: Fund guidelines say that an option premium must be at least 4 percent of the underlying stock price, with a minimum of 2 1/2 percent upside potential

rule.action: filter covered calls
rule.notes: Example fund's mandate (not universal); make configurable.

principles.principle: When current IV is very low versus normal, call writers earn below-normal premiums and overwriting guidelines may be hard to meet.
principles.quote: By contrast, current risk is very low, particularly compared to this chart’s “normal” readings, so traders who write calls against the stock will earn below-normal premiums.

rule.action: de-prioritize covered call writing; consider buying protection
rule.notes: IBM example also shows IV term structure rising into weak Sep-Oct.

principles.principle: Volatility and trading patterns can change after Fed rate increases or bond-market declines, especially for rate-sensitive sectors.
principles.quote: Trading patterns and volatility levels may change after the Fed increases interest rates, for instance, or after a sharp decline in the bond market.

rule.action: re-evaluate IV assumptions for utilities, industrials

principles.principle: Extreme moves outside the 95% band can be three to five times larger than normal-range moves.
principles.quote: The sharpest movements may be between three and five times greater, or even more, than those in the normal range.

rule.action: stress-test positions at 3-5x normal moves

principles.principle: When data and pricing models become unreliable in extremes, use simple strategies, move slowly and use limit orders.
principles.quote: When these models become unreliable, it’s best to use simple strategies and move slowly.

rule.action: restrict to simple strategies; limit orders only
rule.notes: Limit orders may not fill.

principles.principle: In extremes, value positions at intrinsic (as if at expiration), net long and short exposure, review naked exposure and adjust risk.
principles.quote: Look at intrinsic values and positions, pairing long and short exposure and attempting to net positions as if each option were at expiration. Review your naked exposure (long or short), then adjust your risk.

rule.action: report intrinsic-value exposure and naked exposure

principles.principle: Brokers and regulators may raise margin requirements during high volatility, forcing more capital or position closings.
principles.quote: This may result in higher capital demands and/or position closings.

rule.action: stress-test margin under higher requirements

principles.principle: Sudden extremes and the volatility they create usually do not last long.
principles.quote: the extremes (and the volatility and risk levels they create) don’t usually last very long.

rule.action: avoid long-dated commitments priced at extreme IV

principles.principle: Prefer exchange-traded, OCC-backed FLEX options to OTC contracts for tailored hedges; OTC hedges may not be recognized as bona fide hedges.
principles.quote: Funds can benefit by using FLEX contracts as an alternative that still fulfills the need for tailored derivatives products.

rule.action: prefer listed/FLEX over OTC

principles.principle: Long calls instead of long stock give leverage at lower cost when borrowing is expensive, especially for higher-priced stocks.
principles.quote: Managers are using long call options instead of long stock positions, which gives them more leverage.

rule.action: suggest call substitution

principles.principle: Buying puts instead of short selling limits loss to the premium no matter how high the stock goes.
principles.quote: Losses are limited to the put’s cost, no matter how high the stock moves.

rule.action: prefer long puts over short stock
rule.notes: Uptick-rule constraints make the case stronger.

principles.principle: Averaging down can take years to pay off and ties up capital (IBM took nearly 10 years to recover from 1987).
principles.quote: constant price averaging can take a long time to pay off.

rule.action: warn; suggest repair strategy instead

principles.principle: Repair a losing stock with a 1x2 bullish call ratio spread several months out: buy one (usually ATM) call and sell two higher (usually OTM) calls per 100 shares, ideally for no added capital.
principles.quote: Most repair strategies involve purchasing a 1-by-2 bullish ratio spread with several months until expiration.

rule.condition: long stock with unrealized loss, expect partial recovery
rule.action: 1x2 call ratio repair; target net credit/zero cost
rule.notes: Lowers breakeven; caps upside at upper strike; must be in margin account (p.132).

principles.principle: The repair strategy may be appropriate when market conditions change abruptly.
principles.quote: This strategy may be appropriate when market conditions abruptly change.

rule.action: offer repair strategy

principles.principle: Use liquid U.S. markets (ETFs, ADRs, indices, currency options) to hedge global positions, especially when foreign markets are closed or abnormal.
principles.quote: Using the U.S. markets to hedge global positions may be a practical choice, especially during periods of abnormal market activity.

rule.action: hedge via U.S.-listed proxies

principles.principle: Leveraged, inverse and leveraged-inverse ETFs are poor hedges: daily rebalancing, tracking problems and misleading margin/risk treatment.
principles.quote: Leveraged, inverse, and leveraged inverse ETFs, however, are typically not good risk management vehicles, in my opinion.

rule.action: block/warn

principles.principle: Hedging low-IV stocks is easy, but repeatedly re-buying hedges on a stock that fails to appreciate can cost more than the gain.
principles.quote: If the share price fails to appreciate and the hedge must be reimplemented over and over, however, the cost of that protection may counter any potential gain.

rule.condition: cumulative hedge cost vs unrealized gain
rule.action: warn: hedge cost exceeding benefit

principles.principle: Use the volatility skew (IV across expirations) to judge whether premiums are relatively cheap or expensive over the hedge period.
principles.quote: A volatility skew is a useful tool in this situation, as it indicates whether option premiums are relatively cheap or expensive over a given period of time.

rule.action: select expiry where ATM IV is relatively cheap

principles.principle: Implied volatility is typically higher for spot-month contracts, which react more to short-term movement.
principles.quote: Implied volatility is typically higher for spot-month contracts, because their values are more affected by short-term movements than are those of longer-term contracts.

rule.action: expect front-month IV premium; inverted structure = event/seasonal risk

principles.principle: Look at a range of puts and calculate break-even points before choosing a hedge.
principles.quote: Look at a range of puts and calculate the break-even points for purchasing contracts.

rule.action: tabulate strike, bid/ask, IV, delta, breakeven, % to breakeven per expiry (Table 14.1)
rule.notes: Include theta to show near-term decay.

principles.principle: ITM puts have higher delta but are expensive; deep-ITM puts further diminish leverage.
principles.quote: Deep in-the-money contracts further diminish leverage quality.

rule.action: de-prioritize deep ITM puts

principles.principle: ATM puts (delta about 40-55%) are probably the best hedge vehicles given their cost offset.
principles.quote: These contracts may not provide strong protection over the next point or two, but given the cost offset, they are probably the best hedge vehicles.

rule.action: default to ATM puts (|delta| 0.40-0.55)

principles.principle: OTM puts are cheap 'catastrophic protection' with low delta and little protection in the first points of a decline.
principles.quote: This means that they may offer little or no real protection during the first several points of a decline.

rule.action: label OTM puts as catastrophic protection only

principles.principle: Avoid roughly one-month hedges, which cost more than two-month contracts per unit of time and must be rebought frequently.
principles.quote: Most managers would avoid the 32-day contracts, since those contracts would be more expensive than the two-month contracts.

rule.action: prefer >= 2-month hedge expiries
rule.notes: 45-day cutoff is an implementation interpolation between the book's 32-day and 60-day examples.

principles.principle: Strike/expiry by profile: conservative = three-month ATM put; slightly aggressive = two-month ATM; protecting against a sharp decline = three-month OTM.
principles.quote: Conservative managers who want minimum losses at a manageable cost would likely purchase the three-month puts with the $55 strike

rule.action: choose put per risk profile
rule.notes: PG example breakevens 5.2% and 4.3% below price.

principles.principle: Protective puts work well when premiums are relatively low; when they are not, consider a collar.
principles.quote: Protective puts work well, especially when premiums are relatively low.

rule.condition: IV low -> protective put; IV high -> collar
rule.action: hedge selection by IV

principles.subsection: Collar Hedges for Long Stock Positions
principles.principle: A collar buys a protective put at high IV and writes an OTM call to pay for it; use it when you expect the stock to stay between the strikes and accept capped upside.
principles.quote: A collar, also referred to as a “hedge wrapper,” lets a manager purchase a protective put with high implied volatility levels by also writing an out-of-the-money call

rule.condition: long stock, IV high, expected range-bound
rule.action: long OTM/ATM put + short OTM call

principles.subsection: Collar Hedges for Long Stock Positions
principles.principle: Collars suit periods without expected market-moving news (e.g., travel), seasonal protection, or protection ahead of earnings/negative news.
principles.quote: Some managers use this strategy seasonally; others use it as protection against an upcoming earnings report or other, potentially negative news.

rule.condition: earnings or seasonal weak period ahead
rule.action: suggest collar

principles.subsection: Collar Hedges for Long Stock Positions
principles.principle: Put premiums above 10% of the stock price significantly reduce a protective put's effectiveness; a near-zero-cost collar is the better choice.
principles.quote: put premiums exceeded 10 percent of the stock price. This significantly reduces the effectiveness of the protected put strategy hedge.

rule.action: switch from protective put to collar
rule.notes: JCP example: ~6-month, put ~9% OTM, call ~10% OTM, $0.35 net debit.

principles.subsection: Other Hedges for Offsetting High Volatility Levels
principles.principle: A bear put spread hedge offsets the high cost of an ATM put without capping upside, but protects only between the strikes.
principles.quote: By using this strategy, managers can purchase protection without capping the stock’s upside potential—a significant advantage.

rule.condition: IV high, expected decline limited to a floor
rule.action: long ATM put + short OTM put at expected floor
rule.notes: Some use it only on low-HV stocks. Example: 1-month, before earnings.

principles.subsection: Other Hedges for Offsetting High Volatility Levels
principles.principle: To cut hedge cost further, buy one put per 100 shares and sell two lower-strike puts (1x2), which acts like a low-limit buy order but has uncapped risk below the lower strike.
principles.quote: consider a ratio spread that involves purchasing one put contract for each 100 shares of the underlying stock that the position is long, then selling two contracts against each 100 shares.

rule.condition: IV high, willing to add shares lower
rule.action: 1x2 put ratio hedge
rule.notes: Below lower strike, loses 2 points per point (p.146); requires naked option approval.

principles.subsection: Other Hedges for Offsetting High Volatility Levels
principles.principle: Use ratio spreads only within a month or two of expiration to limit downside liability and benefit from time decay.
principles.quote: Smart managers often use ratio spreads only within a month or two before option expiration.

rule.action: restrict ratio-spread hedges to <= ~2 months

principles.subsection: Other Hedges for Offsetting High Volatility Levels
principles.principle: Ratio-spread portfolio hedges' risk may outweigh benefits in a 30%+ decline; manage actively.
principles.quote: The risk of the strategy may outweigh the benefits if the market drops 30 percent or more. Actively manage the position.

rule.action: stress-test; warn on ratio hedges
rule.notes: QQQQ example second breakeven ~29% down.

principles.subsection: Other Hedges for Offsetting High Volatility Levels
principles.principle: If the market does not decline over time, cover at least the naked portion of the ratio spread to free margin.
principles.quote: If the market does not decline as time progresses, consider covering at least the naked portion of the ratio spread.

rule.action: buy back extra short puts

principles.principle: Stock replacement candidates: positions bought within the past six months that gained 10-50% or more, whose seasonal strength is ending or appreciation is slowing.
principles.quote: find a purchase that your fund made during the past six months that has appreciated significantly: between 10 and 50 percent or more, depending on market conditions.

rule.condition: held <= 6 months AND gain between 10% and 50%+
rule.action: flag as stock replacement candidate
rule.notes: Also: seasonally strong period ending or appreciation rate slowing.

principles.principle: Sell the shares and buy an ITM or ATM call to remove capital and most profit while keeping upside, limiting risk to the premium.
principles.quote: By selling the shares and replacing the stock with an in-the-money or at-the-money call contract, you remove the original capital commitment, plus the majority of the unrealized profits.

rule.action: sell stock; buy ITM/ATM call
rule.notes: IBM example: 2-month $115 call with stock $117.02.

principles.principle: Long-stock hedge choice by IV (Figure 15.1): low IV favors protective puts and collars; mid IV bear put spreads and covered calls; high IV bear call spreads and bear ratio put spreads.
principles.quote: Long stock hedging strategies that are based on implied volatility/option premium levels.

rule.action: select hedge structure by IV level
rule.notes: Order read from Figure 15.1 labels (approximate positions). Text elsewhere uses collars for high IV (p.142), so treat collar as low-to-mid.

principles.principle: ETF options (SPY, IWM) are generally better portfolio hedges than index options: cheaper, multi-exchange, tailorable, American-style; index options settle in cash.
principles.quote: the ETF market’s widespread acceptance has made products such as the S&P Depository Trust (SPY) and iSHARES Russell 2000 Index Fund (IWM) generally better choices for fund managers.

rule.action: default to ETF options; note index cash settlement
rule.notes: SPX hedge had slightly higher recapture but cost more and is less liquid.

principles.principle: Portfolio hedge: pick a highly correlated index/ETF, avoid too-short expirations, use ATM or slightly OTM puts.
principles.quote: Choose the hedge period, but don’t choose a contract that expires too quickly, as the time decay erodes the value. Next choose an at-the-money or slightly out-of-the-money strike price.

rule.action: buy puts on correlated ETF/index
rule.notes: Example cost ~3.3-3.4% of portfolio for 2-month ATM.

principles.principle: Number of hedge contracts = (portfolio value x correlation) / (index or ETF price x 100); used for puts on long portfolios and calls on short portfolios.
principles.quote: Now comes the hard part: deciding how many put contracts to purchase.

rule.action: compute hedge contract count
rule.notes: Formula printed p.158; same formula for short-portfolio call hedge (p.166).

principles.principle: Judge hedge effectiveness by recapture rate (hedge gain / portfolio loss); above 75% on a 20% decline is good.
principles.quote: A 100 percent recapture rate is probably impossible, but recapture rates above 75 percent on a 20 percent portfolio decline are good.

rule.action: accept hedge if recapture > 75% at -20%
rule.notes: Recapture low at -5% as premium is absorbed.

principles.principle: Hedges get expensive near market peaks, on negative news and late summer; September is historically the worst month (average -0.5%).
principles.quote: September is historically the worst month of the year, with an average decline of 0.5 percent, though that decline doesn’t happen every year.

rule.action: expect elevated hedge cost; consider cost-reduction structures

principles.principle: When premiums rise, write a call above the current index level against the long put.
principles.quote: Consider writing a call against the long put purchase with a strike that’s above the current index level.

rule.action: add short OTM call (portfolio collar)

principles.principle: Keep hedge length short around the October-to-November seasonal turn so the hedge does not evaporate when the market turns up.
principles.quote: This is one reason that you may want to keep hedge length short: There’s no sense in buying a hedge, only to see the market turn around and the strategy evaporate.

rule.condition: hedge during weak season ending October
rule.action: set hedge expiry around end of seasonal weakness

principles.principle: After a significant drop with recovery expected, scale out of the hedge near the estimated low and close the rest once a rebound is confirmed.
principles.quote: begin selling part of the hedge position near your estimated low point. Keep working the hedge until you are convinced that a rebound is at hand, then close the remaining hedge position.

rule.condition: near estimated low after significant drop
rule.action: scale out of hedge; close on confirmed rebound

principles.principle: When hedge premiums are too steep (e.g., 4.9% of the ETF for two months), use a portfolio collar to cut cost while keeping some upside.
principles.quote: A portfolio collar strategy may help reduce costs while still providing some upside potential.

rule.action: add short OTM call (collar)
rule.notes: XLK example: selling ~7% OTM call cut cost 47%.

principles.principle: Managers reluctant to write calls can use a bear put spread or ratio bear spread; writing an OTM put against the long put reduces cost.
principles.quote: Regardless of your choice, writing an out-of-the-money put against a long put may reduce your cost.

rule.condition: hedge cost high, no call writing allowed
rule.action: put spread or 1x2 put ratio
rule.notes: Ratio bear for those expecting only a limited decline.

principles.principle: In a rising-rate/inflation scenario, overweight or buy calls on commodity/energy stocks, buy puts on construction/real estate (e.g., XHB), and sell calls on retail (XRT).
principles.quote: By overweighting or purchasing calls on these stocks, they may benefit from increasing demand for these companies or their products as the tightening cycle progresses.

rule.action: long commodity/energy calls; homebuilder puts; retail short calls; plus portfolio hedge

principles.principle: When volatility is above average, writing OTM puts lets a fund benefit from time and premium decay.
principles.quote: When volatility levels are above average, writing out-of-the-money puts may result in minimal gains while also letting a fund benefit from the progression of time and option premium decay.

rule.action: write OTM puts

principles.principle: Multi-leg hedges get confusing; monitor aggregate portfolio movement and each piece, with relative performance and momentum.
principles.quote: Monitor the aggregate portfolio movement as well as the pieces.

rule.action: aggregate and per-leg P&L/greeks

principles.principle: Short portfolios are harder to hedge: volatility rises as prices fall (hedges get expensive) and shorts can be bought in.
principles.quote: It is more difficult to hedge short positions than it is to hedge long positions, for two reasons.

rule.action: warn on short-portfolio hedge cost

principles.principle: Hedge a short portfolio by buying calls (sized with the same formula) when the market has risen and IV has dropped.
principles.quote: If the market has appreciated and implied volatility has dropped, buying a call might be a good hedging strategy.

rule.condition: short portfolio AND market up AND IV down
rule.action: buy ~2-month ATM calls on correlated ETF
rule.notes: DIA example: cost 2.5% of portfolio, ~72% recapture at +13%.

principles.principle: If IV is high when hedging shorts, use a bull call spread or sell an OTM put to offset the long call's cost.
principles.quote: A manager could implement an offsetting bull spread, selling an out-of-the-money call to offset the cost of the purchased call. Or a manager could sell an out-of-the-money put.

rule.condition: short portfolio hedge with high IV
rule.action: bull call spread or long call + short OTM put

principles.principle: Swap short stock positions into long puts, short calls, or both, to reduce buy-in and rebate risk and earn time decay.
principles.quote: A manager could also close the short positions and swap them into long puts, short calls, or a combination.

rule.action: replace short stock with puts/short calls
rule.notes: Use individual strategies for holdings with worst momentum/RS.

principles.principle: Use trailing stops to limit reversal risk on short portfolios.
principles.quote: Use trailing stops to limit reversal risk.

rule.action: attach trailing stops
rule.notes: No trailing distance given.

principles.principle: Hedge commodity exposure with highly correlated ETFs: USO for crude oil, UNG for natural gas, GLD for gold, GDX for gold miners.
principles.quote: It’s easy to hedge oil by using the US Oil Fund LP (USO), an ETF that has a very high correlation to light sweet crude oil futures.

rule.action: use commodity ETF options for hedges
rule.notes: Correlations between markets change; verify.

principles.principle: If rates are expected to rise, buy puts on a long-Treasury ETF (TLT) or use CBOE rate index options (IRX, FVX, TNX, TYX).
principles.quote: Buy put options if you think interest rates are going higher, because the fund price typically moves lower when rates increase.

rule.action: rate hedge
rule.notes: Rate indices are 10x the yield.

principles.principle: Include all positions in hedge analysis; build at least a spreadsheet of current and projected values under market moves.
principles.quote: As you create hedges, make sure that you include all your positions in your analysis.

rule.action: scenario grid of all positions
rule.notes: Projections depend on volatility assumptions.

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: Stocks lead the economy by three to six months or more, so investors waiting for economic confirmation enter and exit late.
principles.quote: In most instances, however, stocks lead the economy by three to six months or more, so many investors enter and exit their positions late.

rule.action: rely on price/breadth over economic data
rule.notes: Months.

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: A rising percentage of NYSE stocks above their 200-day MA confirms an investable uptrend; turn more aggressive when it breaks above 50%; with high IV use covered combinations and put writing.
principles.quote: taken a more aggressive position in June, after NYSEPAUS (Bloomberg symbol for NYSE shares above their 200-day moving averages) broke above the 50 percent level.

rule.action: increase bullish exposure (via covered combos/short puts if IV high)

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: Percent of NYSE stocks above their 200-day MA: above 50% is positive; near 90% the rally may be overextended, so look for overbought groups.
principles.quote: A reading above 50 percent is positive, signaling that more than half the issues on the “Big Board” are positive. A reading near 90 percent suggests that the rally may be overextended.

rule.action: >50 bullish; ~90 overextended -> hedge/overwrite overbought groups

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: The beginning of a trend is the riskiest time to invest; if IV is high, write OTM puts instead of buying shares.
principles.quote: If implied volatility levels are high, consider writing out-of-the-money put contracts instead of buying shares, to help balance risk and reward.

rule.condition: new trend beginning AND IV high
rule.action: short OTM put instead of buying stock
rule.notes: New trend after a sharp bear market may carry relatively low risk.

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: Or buy a quarter (to half) position and sell an equal number of OTM calls and puts with two to six months to expiration.
principles.quote: Managers could also buy a quarter position in the stock and sell an equivalent number of out-of-the-money calls and puts with between two and six months until expiration.

rule.action: covered combination
rule.notes: Example: IV ~150%, 2-month, call ~28% OTM, put ~23% OTM.

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: New bull market signs: improving advance-decline and up-volume, fewer new lows, stocks/sectors above rising 50-day MAs, and VIX falling to about half its 52-week range (all lagging).
principles.quote: Implied volatility, as measured by the CBOE S&P 500 Implied Volatility Index (VIX) and other volatility indicators, drops to about half of its range for the past 52 weeks.

rule.condition: VIX <= ~50% of 52-week range AND price > rising SMA50 AND breadth improving
rule.action: confirm new bull market

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: Once established, an intermediate-term uptrend of more than two months emerges, the advance broadens, new highs expand, and more stocks rise above 50- then 200-day MAs with higher lows then higher highs.
principles.quote: In most cases a positive intermediate-term trend of more than two months emerges, volume returns, and the advance broadens.

rule.condition: uptrend duration > 2 months AND breadth broadening
rule.action: confirm established trend
rule.notes: IV declines and skew improves.

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: It is unwise to declare market bottoms or tops while events are in progress.
principles.quote: It’s unwise to declare market bottoms or tops while events are in progress

rule.action: avoid top/bottom calls; wait for confirmation

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: For a short-dated just-ITM call, set an option-price target and stop (example: $1.75 call, target $4.50, stop $1.15).
principles.quote: I suggested an initial option target of $4.50 and a stop at $1.15.

rule.action: set target ~+157% and stop ~-34% of premium (example)
rule.notes: Ratios derived from one example; make configurable.

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: A longer-dated ITM call (delta ~70%) gives long exposure with about 83% less capital at risk than stock.
principles.quote: This option puts the would-be buyer in a long position, but with capital risk that’s approximately 83 percent lower than the capital risk of buying stock.

rule.action: buy ITM call (~0.70 delta), longest practical expiry

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: After the stock rises, write OTM calls against the long calls, or roll to a higher strike while selling a portion to remove capital risk.
principles.quote: Or swap the call with a $20 strike into one with a $30 or $35 strike, selling a portion of the position to remove capital risk or take profits.

rule.condition: long call position after substantial rise
rule.action: write OTM calls against long calls or roll up and scale out
rule.notes: Remember seasonal factors.

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: Sideways and bear markets are usually trading markets because investors cannot succeed in momentum-less ranges or major downtrends.
principles.quote: Sideways and bear markets are usually trading markets, because most investors cannot succeed in longer sideways markets, which lack momentum, or through major downward trends.

rule.action: switch to trading mode (shorter horizons, oscillator-driven option trades)

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: In trading markets, sell calls on overbought issues and puts on oversold issues as alternatives to selling or buying shares, especially when premiums are elevated.
principles.quote: Selling calls on overbought issues or selling puts on oversold issues may provide alternatives to selling or buying shares, especially when premiums are elevated.

rule.condition: trading market AND overbought (sell call) / oversold (sell put) AND IV elevated
rule.action: short call on overbought; short put on oversold

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: Stops or real hedges are better risk controls than selling an opposing option.
principles.quote: (Stops or real hedges are even better ways to control risk.)

rule.action: use stop or true hedge

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: Upper Bollinger Band test plus overbought RSI, a momentum divergence and low IV in a choppy stock: buy a put or bear put spread (investors use it as a hedge without capping upside).
principles.quote: Traders could take advantage of a potential correction by purchasing a put or bear spread using puts.

rule.condition: close at upper band AND RSI overbought AND momentum lower high AND IV low
rule.action: buy put or bear put spread
rule.notes: KFT example.

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: Confirmed signals: RSI changes direction and crosses above 30; stochastic %K crosses %D; waiting for them can miss sudden moves.
principles.quote: The RSI’s signals confirm when the indicator changes direction and crosses above 30 percent. The stochastic oscillator’s signal occurs when %K crosses %D.

rule.action: confirmed buy signal

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: In a rising trend with diminishing momentum (or dropping volume), write an OTM call, since a consolidation or minor correction is more likely than a decline, especially for leaders; check relative performance.
principles.quote: In a rising trend with diminishing momentum, it may be more appropriate to write an out-of-the-money call, because shares may enter a consolidation or very minor correction instead of a decline.

rule.action: write OTM covered call

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: Buying a put against a long position may help when volatility rises, but one contract per 100 shares may not offset share losses in the short term.
principles.quote: it may be very difficult to offset a share’s position loss if you buy one contract for each 100 shares, at least in the short term.

rule.action: show delta-adjusted hedge coverage

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: Leader/follower pairs in the same sector: take a negative position in the overbought leader near resistance and a positive position in the lagger; not for special situations like takeover targets.
principles.quote: A trader may identify overbought stocks or those nearing resistance and take a negative position on that issue and a positive position in the lagging shares.

rule.action: short leader leg / long laggard leg (options)
rule.notes: Exclude acquisition targets or pending-news names.

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: Look for divergences between relative performance, RSI and price; momentum rolling off its peak while price rises means the advance is losing steam.
principles.quote: (In most situations, managers should look for divergences.)

rule.condition: price higher high AND indicator lower high
rule.action: flag divergence

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: Pair example: buy calls on the strengthening sector ETF and write calls on the stalled leader; close after the ETF's worst one-day performance in months / overbought correction.
principles.quote: An astute trader would have likely closed the position on May 8, following XRT’s worst one-day performance in months.

rule.condition: pair open; ETF worst daily return in months
rule.action: close pair

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: Monitor pair and trading strategies closely; check execution, margin and interest costs and whether the mandate permits the trade.
principles.quote: Check execution costs, margin requirements, and interest costs, which may significantly reduce a strategy’s value.

rule.action: include costs and mandate checks

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: Candlestick reversal signals are stronger when confirmed by oscillators, and signals on longer-term charts are more significant.
principles.quote: These signals are stronger when they’re combined with other, similar signals from an oscillator or other technical gauge.

rule.action: weight weekly > daily signals
rule.notes: Reversal candles may signal a halt/sideways rather than countertrend.

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: A weekly bearish engulfing candle ending an overbought trend channel with high IV (~81%) suits a 1x2 bear put ratio spread with max profit at the lower strike.
principles.quote: Traders may have purchased a bear ratio spread, buying the July 75 puts and selling the July 65 puts for a $2.40 net debit on a 1-by-2 basis.

rule.condition: weekly bearish engulfing AND IV high
rule.action: 1x2 put ratio (long ~ATM, 2 short ~13% lower)
rule.notes: Below lower strike profit erodes point-for-point.

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: Long holders after a weekly reversal can use a longer-dated, near-zero-cost collar.
principles.quote: A longer time frame might have worked well, perhaps including a collar strategy using August options.

rule.action: collar (example: call ~20% OTM, put ~13% OTM, net credit)

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: Expiration pinning: higher open interest at a strike raises the probability that the stock pins there; scan candidates from Tuesday of expiration week.
principles.quote: The higher the open interest level, which shows the number of outstanding contracts, the greater the probability that pinning will take place.

rule.condition: expiration week; concentrated OI at a strike near price
rule.action: identify pin strike (start Tuesday of expiration week)

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: If the pin strike is above the price, buy a call bull spread with the short call at the pin strike; if below, buy a higher-strike ITM put and sell a put at the pin strike.
principles.quote: we would buy a bull spread with a call at a low strike and sell a call with the target strike price.

rule.action: vertical spread with short leg at pin strike

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: Selling the straddle at the pin strike requires remaining time premium; beware acquisitions, ex-dividends and earnings.
principles.quote: To make the practice worthwhile, make sure that the contracts have some time premium.

rule.action: require time value; block if takeover/ex-div/earnings imminent

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: Long holders above the pin strike can write OTM calls one month beyond the upcoming expiration; to add, write a put at the pin strike with an extra month or buy just above the strike.
principles.quote: Consider writing out-of-the-money calls against stock shares when the stock is above the pinning strike price. Go out another month from the upcoming expiration to collect some premium.

rule.action: write next-month OTM call; or sell next-month put at pin strike
rule.notes: Place buy order just above the strike.

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: Buy straddles/strangles before expected announcements, sometimes weeks ahead; buying earlier (before IV inflates) was more profitable.
principles.quote: Traders may purchase straddles or strangles before an expected announcement—sometimes weeks ahead, to benefit from a possibly early announcement or from stock moves ahead of a release date.

rule.condition: event ahead AND IV not yet inflated
rule.action: buy straddle/strangle weeks ahead
rule.notes: ARNA: IV went from ~70% to 246% before event.

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: Manage long straddles/strangles by selling calls as the stock moves higher and puts as it moves lower.
principles.quote: Managers might sell calls when the stock is moving higher and sell puts when the stock is moving lower.

rule.action: scale out of winning leg

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: Investors facing a binary event with high IV can write OTM calls against stock bought near lows, or sell the stock and sell OTM puts to repurchase lower.
principles.quote: With ARNA’s implied volatility levels high, the holder could have sold the stock and the October 4 puts at $1.00.

rule.condition: binary event ahead AND IV very high
rule.action: covered call, or sell stock + short OTM put

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: M&A announcements push premiums sharply higher, then they contract (absent rival bids or blocking risk); cash-deal targets trade in a narrowing range.
principles.quote: Any merger or acquisition announcement, regardless of its fine print, often pushes options premiums sharply higher.

rule.action: expect IV spike then contraction; cash deal -> narrowing sideways

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: In stock-swap mergers, buy the acquirer and sell the target when there is an economic difference; discrepancies vanish as the deal matures.
principles.quote: In a merger paid for through a stock swap, traders may benefit by purchasing the acquiring company and selling the company being acquired, if there is an economic difference between the two values.

rule.action: merger arbitrage pair

principles.chapter: When to Invest, When to Trade
principles.principle: Swap a target holding into a synthetic long (sell stock, buy call, sell put); a short in the acquirer can become a synthetic short when borrow is scarce or rebates jump.
principles.quote: This trade may be a good choice when there is a shortage of stock to be loaned, or when rebate fees are expected to jump sharply.

rule.action: use synthetic short (short call + long put) instead of short stock

principles.principle: Use clean, reliable long- and short-term data; garbage data create useless charts.
principles.quote: Technical analysis uses graphs as a basis for making decisions, and garbage data create useless graphs.

rule.action: validate price data (gaps, splits, bad prints) before signals

principles.principle: Screen holdings for RSI or stochastic overbought readings to find covered-call candidates.
principles.quote: including writing calls against long stock positions when the relative strength index (RSI) or stochastic oscillators indicate overbought conditions.

rule.action: scan and rank covered-call candidates
rule.notes: Also screens: candlestick signals, volume breakouts.

principles.principle: Unusual options volume or sharp IV increases (checked for bid vs offer side) have produced signals before news such as acquisitions.
principles.quote: At times this report has produced signals before news events, including acquisition announcements.

rule.condition: option volume multiple of average AND/OR IV jump
rule.action: flag unusual activity; check trade side
rule.notes: Figure 17.8 reports volume as multiple of average daily volume and put/call ratio.

principles.principle: Monitor positions with real-time P&L and delta, gamma and vega per position and in aggregate, with scenario analysis by price and date.
principles.quote: It offers some risk analysis, including delta, gamma, and vega information for each position and in the aggregate.

rule.action: aggregate greeks + price/date scenario grid

principles.principle: Track current implied volatility against its 52-week high and low.
principles.quote: It shows changing implied volatility values and their respective 52-week

rule.action: compute IV rank/percentile
